learning_objective: 🎯 Roll into the world of perfect curves! Master the geometry of circles, chords, arcs, and the incredible angles hidden inside cyclic quadrilaterals.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A circle is a collection of points at a fixed distance (Radius) from the center. A line connecting two points on the circle is a 'Chord'. The longest chord passes through the center and is called the 'Diameter'.
If you draw a straight line perfectly at 90° (perpendicular) from the center of the circle to any chord, it will slice that chord into two exactly equal halves (bisect it).
An arc is a piece of the circle's curve. The angle an arc makes at the exact center of the circle is always DOUBLE the angle it makes at any point on the remaining edge of the circle.

If all 4 corners of a quadrilateral touch the edge of a circle, it is a 'Cyclic Quadrilateral'. Its magical property is that opposite angles will always add up to exactly 180° (they are supplementary).

fun_activity.title: 📐 The Semi-Circle Illusion
fun_activity.instructions: Draw a perfect circle and a diameter straight across it. Pick ANY point on the top edge of the circle and draw lines connecting it to both ends of the diameter. Measure the angle you just made at the top. It will ALWAYS be exactly 90°, no matter where you put the point! (Angle in a semi-circle is a right angle).

exam_tips: 📌 'Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.' If you see two chords of the same length, their angles at the center are identical.
📌 Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. This is heavily used to find missing 'x' and 'y' values in circle diagrams.
📌 For a Cyclic Quadrilateral, opposite angles add to 180°. If $\angle A = 100^\circ$, then $\angle C$ strictly must be $80^\circ$.
quick_recap: ⭐ A chord is a line segment linking two points on a circle; the diameter is the longest chord.
⭐ A perpendicular drawn from the center to a chord perfectly bisects that chord.
⭐ In a cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of either pair of opposite angles is exactly 180°.
